457 British service personnel died in Afghanistan. They died serving their country and I am in awe of their sacrifice and bravery. They all left behind families, friends and loved ones who, to this day, will feel their absence and the deep sense of loss that stays with them.

Our troops were in Afghanistan because we, with our NATO allies, answered the US call when they triggered (the only time it has been triggered) Article 5 after 9/11. The President should remember that we stood alongside America during that dark time and many of our braver service personnel lost their lives in that call.   

The President should know better and show a little respect.   

Today I am remembering the brave service personnel who gave their lives while serving our country. Locally, we rightly named streets after eight men who gave their lives in Afghanistan. Just off Europa Way, you will see eight streets named after these men.   

Conrad Lewis Way, named after Private Conrad Lewis who lost his life in 2011 while on patrol in the Nad-e Ali district of Helmand province. He was 22.

Mentors can have a transformational effect on your life, they certainly did on mine. 

Many people have a narrow view of what mentorship really means. They often picture a mentor as a high-flying businessperson who spares you five or ten minutes of their time, points you in the right direction, and that’s it. If you’re lucky, maybe they’ll give you a bit more.

But real mentorship is much deeper than that— they are all around you and touch your life in many ways, often without you even realizing it.

For example, you’re three times more likely to start a business if your parents have their own business. That’s not just coincidence—it’s because you grow up in an environment where risk-taking is encouraged and running your own business is seen as normal. That was true for me. My, first mentor, my dad encouraged all of us to go into business, and we all did. He showed us what was possible when you work for yourself.

My next mentor was John Waterhouse, my business partner. He had faith in me during a really tough time in my life. I’d lost my job and was working in a video shop, and yet he still believed I could be a good business partner. We set up our company together in 1992, and he taught me a huge amount about business.

Another key mentor for me was my sister, Glyn. Mentors like her open your eyes to what’s possible—not just in the world, but within yourself. She gave me the confidence to take our small business, which had just a handful of offices, and grow it into a national network of 200 locations. She saw potential in me before I saw it myself, and she was able to communicate that belief in a way that really stuck.

Finally, there’s Harry Hill—not the comedian, but the former CEO of Countrywide, the UK’s largest estate agency. I met him after the financial crash, when our business was in real trouble. A few years later, I persuaded him to join us as a non-executive director. He completely transformed our business. At the time, it might have been worth a few m

Today the government announced a new Child Poverty Strategy, a historic step I’ve long called for and one I’m genuinely pleased to see. 

It takes a whole-system approach, tackling the root causes of child poverty across three key areas.

💷 Boosting family incomes
Families deserve the resources to meet their children’s needs through higher wages, fairer work and a stronger social security safety net. I am especially pleased to see the removal of the two-child limit, the biggest driver of rising child poverty. This change alone will lift 450,000 children out of poverty by the end of this Parliament.

🏫 Reducing the cost of essentials
Free school meals, breakfast clubs, energy bill support, affordable housing and 30 hours of free childcare will help families cover the basics. Together, these measures will support another 100,000 children, giving families the practical help they need to thrive.

📉 Tackling deep material poverty
For the first time, the government will measure and act on children going without essentials such as three meals a day or a damp-free home.

🏛 My work on this issue
I have consistently raised child poverty in Parliament, including during debates on the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Bill, and through roundtables and school visits with organisations such as Red Door, Caritas and Citizens Advice.

📊 The impact
Altogether, this strategy will lift 550,000 children out of relative low income and help 7.1 million households see their incomes rise, including 1.4 million children in deep material poverty. This is the largest reduction by any government in a single Parliament.

🌱 Tackling child poverty is not just a moral duty. It is an investment in Britain’s future. Every child deserves the chance to thrive, and I remain committed to doing all I can to make that a reality.

It was a pleasure to join Avon Fire & Rescue Service  Red Watch at Temple Fire Station last Friday to celebrate the actions of Firefighters Lee Parsons, Nik Tucker, Matt Pember and Michal Kotlewski in saving the life of a young man in my constituency a few weeks ago.
 
Red Watch were driving along Stapleton Road when they were flagged down by local people in the immediate aftermath of a stabbing. Despite potential risks to their own safety they immediately leapt into action, managing the scene and stabilising the victim until specialist services could arrive, then liaising with them. Without their swift action it's likely the victim would have died at the scene. It was above and beyond the call of duty and I was proud to help present them with the Chief Fire Officer’s Certificate of Commendation, alongside Matt Cook, the Chief Fire Officer, and Paul Goggin, Chair of the Fire Authority.
 
We also spoke about the challenges the Fire and Rescue Service is facing around funding and, in particular, the cap on their precept. I will be writing to the relevant minister to raise this with them.

I want to share something genuinely uplifting that I saw in Norwich the other weekend.

Jade Hunter, the headteacher at West Earlham Infant and Nursery School, told me about an extraordinary act of kindness led by two people, Annie Jennings and Lewis Wardale.

In the weeks before Christmas, Annie and Lewis decided to raise money to support children at the school. Donations began to come in, and it soon became clear their efforts could go further than they first planned. What started as help for a few children became support for the whole school.

Lewis ran 80 km, and Annie cycled 300km. Between them, they raised around £7,000, thanks to generous public contributions.

That support has now become Christmas hampers filled with gifts and toys for every child at the school.

For many families, especially those on fixed incomes, Christmas can be stressful and expensive. These hampers have lifted a real weight from parents’ shoulders. As Jade said, “Every parent wants their child to have a magical Christmas, and this has helped make that possible.”

When I arrived to help pack the hampers, the room was full of Annie and Lewis's friends and family, along with school staff. What could have felt overwhelming turned into something special. A proper community effort.

It shows what people can achieve when they look out for one another. Thank you to everyone involved. This is the very best of Norwich.

When the cenotaph was unveiled in 1920, Whitehall had to be closed for a week as more than a million people filed past in silent tribute, burying the base of the memorial in flowers, in places ten feet deep.

More than 100,000 war memorials now stand across the United Kingdom, two thirds of them constructed in the years that followed the Great War. Every city, town and village had been affected. The nation was united in its desire - its need - to honour the glorious dead.

In 2025 that war to end all wars has slipped from living memory. Indeed the Second World War is now beginning to do so. Just 8,000 veterans of it remain with us, carrying the memories of that extraordinary struggle.

Yet today we will once again come together, as our forebears did, to remember those who sacrificed everything in the service of our country, in the First World War and in every conflict since. 

It’s a simple, but sacred ceremony that has endured for over a century, led today by His Majesty The King at the Cenotaph and replicated at every memorial, from our greatest cities to our quietest hamlets. 

It continues because we know the unpayable debt we owe to those brave servicemen and women who gave the ultimate sacrifice to ensure that we can live in peace and freedom.

We thank the thousands of men and women in uniform today, at home and abroad, who still stand ready to defend us. Men and women who are prepared to pay a price few among us would.

This year, as every year, we wear our poppies with pride. We stand in silent tribute.

And we recommit to building a country worthy of those that gave so much to protect us and the freedoms that have defined it and all those fortunate enough to live on these islands and to call themselves British for centuries.

Renewing Our Armed Forces: From Steel-Cutting to Submarine Recycling

Yesterday I cut steel on HMS Bulldog, the fourth of the Royal Navy’s Type 31 frigates. The next generation of workhorses for the Royal Navy are being built at Rosyth in Scotland. I was there a year ago cutting the first steel on HMS Formidable that is coming together fast. I was also present to see HMS Active, the second of the Inspiration class frigates, roll out of the production shed.

Babcock are best known in Plymouth for running our dockyard but they also build frigates in Rosyth.

As a Government we are investing in our Royal Navy. We are building new Type 26 anti-submarine warfare frigates on the Clyde and Type 31 frigates in Rosyth. They’ll sail alongside new autonomous ships and submarines being trialled in Plymouth where we have the UK’s new National centre for Marine Autonomy. We have increased the number of submarines we want to buy and the last Astute subs and new Dreadnought subs are under construction at Barrow.

In more uncertain times we are investing more of a rising defence budget with British companies. Since the general election we have signed 1100 major defence contracts, 86% with British based firms. We have given our troops the biggest pay rise in 20 years and have published a plan to refit or rebuild 9 in 10 military homes with the first 1,000 worst homes already overhauled.

We are backing veterans with stronger protections in law and record high spending.

I’m proud to be Devonport’s MP and proud to be the son of a Royal Navy submariner. Increasing defence spending is creating more jobs in Plymouth and is why this government has awarded Plymouth not just new town status, but also a defence growth deal and more investment. We are spending £4.4billion on new submarine facilities at Devonport. And I can proudly say Devonport has a bright future ahead of it – no more uncertainty like that we saw over the last decade.

And one more thing, yesterday I got to see the progress

🔵 ⛪️ Last week, I attended the 𝐮𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐟 𝐚 𝐛𝐥𝐮𝐞 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐪𝐮𝐞 𝐚𝐭 Vinecash Presbyterian Church in Portadown, honouring Rev. William Tennent—a Presbyterian minister with deep ties to our community and a legacy that reaches across the Atlantic. 

The Rev Tennent, born in 1673, worshipped in Vinecash before emigrating to America in 1718. His journey and ministry left an extraordinary mark: 𝒉𝒆 𝒊𝒏𝒔𝒑𝒊𝒓𝒆𝒅 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒇𝒐𝒖𝒏𝒅𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒐𝒇 𝑷𝒓𝒊𝒏𝒄𝒆𝒕𝒐𝒏 𝑼𝒏𝒊𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒔𝒊𝒕𝒚 𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒑𝒍𝒂𝒚𝒆𝒅 𝒂 𝒇𝒐𝒖𝒏𝒅𝒂𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒂𝒍 𝒓𝒐𝒍𝒆 𝒊𝒏 𝑨𝒎𝒆𝒓𝒊𝒄𝒂𝒏 𝑷𝒓𝒆𝒔𝒃𝒚𝒕𝒆𝒓𝒊𝒂𝒏𝒊𝒔𝒎.

Tennent came to Northern Ireland as a chaplain for the influential Hamilton family. Following advice to emigrate, he joined the first wave of Ulster settlers to Pennsylvania, where he used his faith and education to create “Log College.” This modest wooden school outside Philadelphia became the model for more than 60 schools and colleges, including Princeton, and ignited a wave of revival known as the Great Awakening.

The plaque at Vinecash commemorates his lasting influence, from his devotion to ministry here in Portadown to his pioneering work in America. As we honour his story, we’re reminded that great things often have humble beginnings. “𝐴𝑛𝑑 𝑙𝑒𝑡 𝑢𝑠 𝑛𝑜𝑡 𝑏𝑒 𝑤𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑦 𝑖𝑛 𝑤𝑒𝑙𝑙 𝑑𝑜𝑖𝑛𝑔: 𝑓𝑜𝑟 𝑖𝑛 𝑑𝑢𝑒 𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑜𝑛 𝑤𝑒 𝑠ℎ𝑎𝑙𝑙 𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑝, 𝑖𝑓 𝑤𝑒 𝑓𝑎𝑖𝑛𝑡 𝑛𝑜𝑡.” (𝐺𝑎𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑛𝑠 6:9, 𝐾𝐽𝑉)

One of the highlights of the day was hearing from Portadown Male Voice Choir during the service - this music was so appropriate and absolutely superb.🎶 🎤

Last Friday I met with the Commonwealth War Graves Commission  in Littleham churchyard, where I met Lizzy from the Commonwealth War Graves Commission and Tim, who volunteers. Tim kindly showed me around the graveyard and shared some of the stories behind those commemorated there.

It was a really moving reminder of the sacrifice made by so many across  #ExmouthandExeterEast . Across the constituency there are 179 commemorations from both World Wars across 27 sites. Of these, 107 are First World War commemorations across 20 sites.

Those remembered served across the Commonwealth: 103 with the United Kingdom, 2 with the Indian Army, and 2 with South Africa. They ranged in age from just 17 to 63 years old.

The work of the Commonwealth War Graves Commission is incredibly important. They care for graves and memorials around the world, ensuring that those who served and gave their lives are remembered with dignity and respect.

Thank you to Lizzy for taking the time to meet with me, and to Tim for the time he gives volunteering and helping visitors learn more about these important sites.

I look forward to continuing to support and advocate for the Commission and their work so that the stories of those who served, and the sacrifices they made, are never forgotten.

An incredible and emotional day in the history of our community - and it nearly didn’t happen.

When I first became an MP, everyone was worried about the future of the Friarage NHS Hospital. The maternity unit had been downgraded, the A&E was under threat, and there were serious doubts about the hospital’s long-term viability. At the time many people thought the Friarage would close.

But after years of uncertainty and relentless campaigning, we’ve finally opened a new Surgical Centre at the Friarage: a world-class facility that secures the hospital’s future, provides a fitting place to work for the fantastic team here and ensures strong local healthcare for generations to come.

It was deeply moving to officially open the building alongside Anne Lamb, an 80-year-old nurse who’s dedicated 34 years of her life to the Friarage. I also enjoyed meeting some of the incredible staff and patients already benefiting from it, including Jason from Catterick who practically ran up to me to share his experience as one of the very first patients here to undergo a hip replacement! His enthusiasm and gratitude underscored exactly why this project matters.

This achievement simply wouldn’t have been possible without the determination of people like Sarah Baker, Head of Clinical Services and lead nurse for the surgical centre. Sarah’s vision, persistence and sheer dedication is transforming patient care - doubling the number of operations, and creating a safer, brighter future for patients across North Yorkshire and beyond.

Enormous credit, too, to James Dunbar, senior consultant at the Friarage, for his enduring passion for this hospital and inspirational leadership.

Finally, special recognition should also go to the Friends of the Friarage, whose unwavering volunteer commitment and fundraising efforts always support improvements in our hospital's services. Their community spirit embodies the very best of North Yorkshire.

Securing the Friarage has always been my top local priori

This picture - a study by Welsh artist Ivor Williams, of Lazarus being raised from the dead - hangs on the walls of Bangor University. The sunlight falling across it caught my eye when I visited recently for a meeting.

Today is Easter Sunday, the day marking  the resurrection of Jesus from the dead. Christians around the world will greet each other with the words "Christ is risen!"

It is a remarkable claim. One that caused even Thomas, the disciple, to doubt - and from which we derive the phrases "doubting Thomas" and "seeing is believing". Many will put ourselves in Thomas' shoes. "Prove it!" we declare - openly with disdain or perhaps inwardly, with hope.

Jesus' reply - a gentle rebuke - was profound "Blessed are those who have not seen but have believed."

And it poses a challenge to us all: can we, who have not seen, also believe? 

We have more evidence of Jesus' existence and teachings than many other contemporary, historical figures. Which makes such words worthy of careful consideration. One writer who did concluded, we really only have three options: Christ was a liar, he was a lunatic - or he was indeed, Lord. 

Ivor Williams reached His own conclusion and produced this painting with a "timeless" message to all ages and backgrounds.

Which conclusion do you think he reached? And which conclusion will you reach?

***Middlesbrough's "forgotten" England manager to be honoured***

Today I was pleased to announce that we've formed a team to create a memorial to the "forgotten" former England manager - Middlesbrough born-and-raised Don Revie - at Archibald Primary School.

Don Revie was a pioneering footballer and coach who won numerous titles on and off the pitch –  a sometimes controversial and divisive figure admittedly - but a man we should take another look at. 

Earlier this year myself and Boro's Fly Me To The Moon fanzine editor Robert Nichols saw an opportunity to apply to local arts body Borderlands for funding for a project to mark Revie’s achievements and inspire pupils at Archibald Primary School. 

Teaming up with the school, local historian Dr Tosh Warwick and Teesside artists Helen and Derek a plan was put forward for a metre-squared mosaic at the school which will be visible to passers by. 

Don Revie was a pioneer in football and his achievements were utterly remarkable. In a very short space of time he took a second division side in Leeds United to the top of the English game and into Europe. 

But whereas others like Brian Clough and Bill Shankly who have had similar achievements are hero figures across the nation, Don Revie is forgotten somewhat outside of Leeds. 

That someone from Middlesbrough’s Newport area could rise to be one of only 16 people to ever hold the permanent position of England football manager and the story not be told seemed to us a crying shame. 

He is a fascinating character who has divided opinion but someone who we should perhaps look again at for the town of Middlesbrough and we hope in this piece of art that we do just that and inspire the pupils of Archibald to know that they can achieve anything they want to. 

Biographies of Don Revie tell the story of how he honed his football skills by going early to Archibald School and practicing by kicking a ball against the playground walls before lessons began.

Borderlands is the Creative

The countdown has begun to celebrations to mark the 500th anniversary of Sutton Coldfield’s Royal charter – and a new organising committee is asking residents for their ideas on how to mark the historic milestone.
2028 will mark 500 years since local benefactor Bishop Vesey persuaded King Henry VIII to grant Sutton Coldfield its famous charter, and this week saw the first meeting of a ‘shadow’ committee which will be responsible for overseeing the planning and development of the arrangements to celebrate the quincentenary.
I am honoured to be chairing the committee, which is led by Royal Sutton Coldfield Town Council (RSCTC) and also includes members from institutions that also trace their histories back to Tudor times, including Bishop Vesey’s Grammar School, Sutton Coldfield Charitable Trust and Holy Trinity Parish Church, where Bishop Vesey is buried.
Other members include a representative of the Friends of Sutton Park Association and Sutton Coldfield Heritage Network and local figures such as Alderman David Roy, who is a member of the Sutton Coldfield Civic Society. The committee will remain a ‘shadow’ committee until after next year’s elections, when long-term political members can be confirmed.

Sutton Coldfield people are proud of our historic town’s Royal status, and 2028 provides a unique opportunity to mark 500 years since it was first granted.
This week marks the beginning of the countdown to celebrations that will not only highlight that rich heritage but will also celebrate today’s Sutton Coldfield and leave a lasting legacy for future generations of Suttonians.
And that’s why we want to hear residents’ own ideas for how we can best celebrate this historic anniversary.
Cllr Simon Ward, Leader of RSCTC, said: “Royal Sutton Coldfield is one of only a handful of Royal towns in the UK, and the 500th anniversary of our historic charter provides an opportunity to celebrate all that is unique about our town. We have a great deal to be proud of in our history a

Fantastic to join Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, Chancellor Rachel Reeves Energy Secretary Ed Miliband, Cllr Louise Gittins - Leader of Cheshire West and Steve Rotheram at the start of a clean energy revolution centred on my Runcorn & Helsby constituency.

They chose the Encirc glass bottling plant, near Elton,Cheshire as the backdrop for a £22 billion funding announcement to decarbonise industry while protecting and creating thousands of jobs.

Projects here and on Teesside in the North East will benefit from this huge investment in carbon capture technology that will catch CO2 emissions for secure storage under the sea.

CO2 created while making the hydrogen here  - plus emissions from other companies like Runcorn-based Viridor - will be caught and stored in the former Liverpool Bay gas fields.

I’m proud my constituency will be at the centre of the clean energy revolution through the HyNet project. We must transition towards a net zero economy if we are to address the climate crisis while sustaining and creating thousands of jobs here and across the region.

The long-term ambition is to produce so-called green hydrogen by splitting water molecules through electrolysis using renewable energy sources, with no carbon dioxide and only oxygen produced. This can be harmlessly vented to the atmosphere.

Yesterday afternoon, a small group gathered in Ashington for their second protest in a month.
The good people of our town have endured enormous challenges over the past century, and many continue to live with the legacy of deindustrialisation and poverty. Frustration with successive governments failing to tackle inequality and crumbling public services is understandable and justified.

But let’s be clear: this protest was never about tackling inequality or fighting for better public services. It was led by a banner that was then displayed in the memorial garden bearing the name of a group identified by Hope not Hate as a neo-Nazi organisation.

Whether or not the organisers understood what this group represents, it is completely unacceptable to have such a banner leading a protest in front of a war memorial, let alone for people to pose for photographs with it. The memorial honours more than 1,000 Ashington residents who gave their lives during the two world wars. Their sacrifice was made in the fight against fascism. To use that sacred space to promote an organisation dedicated to spreading it is nothing short of a desecration.

It is also deeply concerning to see so many young children in attendance, exposed to such hateful imagery and rhetoric. The good people of Ashington deserve better than to have their community and their memorial dragged into association with extremism.

The organisers of this protest should apologise without hesitation for this disgraceful act of disrespect.

On Sunday I stood with our community in remembrance of the seven Czech and Slovak soldiers that lost their lives in completing Operation Anthropoid, the mission to assassinate one of Hitler’s most senior officers, Reinhard Heydrich.

Heydrich was the then Nazi Governor of a large part of Czechoslovakia and the principal architect of the Holocaust.

They carried out their ambush on his staff car on May 27th and, as a result of their attack, which took place in the outskirts of Prague, Heydrich suffered fatal injuries and died on June 4th 1942.

Based in Leamington during the war, the soldiers were part of the several thousand strong Free Czechoslovak Army quartered here and their mission was supported by the RAF with training from the Special Operations Executive.  

Following the attack, the seven went into hiding to avoid capture before their location was betrayed. Despite their extraordinary bravery, they ultimately died in the crypt of a Prague church after a brutal firefight fought by 700 Nazi soldiers. The Nazis then sought retribution by razing several villages and the mass killing of their inhabitants.

Their courageous action and sacrifice is commemorated in the simple but powerful sculpture of a parachute in the heart of Jephson Gardens.

The Slovak Ambassador and senior staff from the Czech embassy were in attendance for what is always a most moving event, made more so by the singing of their respective national anthems by local children - themselves of Slovak and Czech heritage.

STATEMENT ON PROPOSALS FOR A THIRD RUNWAY AT HEATHROW 

Today the Chancellor indicated support in principle for a third runway at Heathrow, without sight of any plans, any analysis of cost, benefits, or impact.
 
The Chancellor is right to prioritise economic growth, and the Government is in desperate need of measures to deliver this, but there is a logical incoherence given the backdrop of the harm to businesses and resulting job losses from their National Insurance tax rise. 
I have been a long-standing opponent of a third runway at Heathrow – while economic growth is important, so are the lives of the people this decision would affect, the environmental implications of such development, and the need to balance growth across the whole of the UK, to name but a few key considerations. ⚽️🥅⚽️ #Billericay Town Women’s Football team ⚽️🥅⚽️

On a chilly night – when it even snowed for a bit! – I visited Vinny from Billericay Town FC Women to see their training sessions in #Billericay with Nick from Essex County FA.

It was fantastic to see such dedication to football from the girls and women that evening – it was absolutely freezing, and it didn’t phase them one bit!

We were chatting about the growth in women’s football, from 1,500 registered players pre-covid across the country to just over 4,000 today. Essex has the largest football contingent in the country, and it really shows when you go to a pub or grassroots game. I’ll be backing Billericay as they look long-term for more support for facilities for football, including for the women’s team.

The team is training well and it shows as they’re in tier 3 of their leagues, higher than many women’s teams from premier league clubs! There is definitely scope for more pitches across Basildon Borough and in Essex, and we really should be investing more into grassroots football. Especially as the health benefits pay dividends long term with keeping more youngsters fit and active.

Worryingly, the Government is currently consulting to remove Sport England as a statutory consultee in planning applications - basically because they stop football pitches being built on. This is so shortsighted and contravenes the Government’s ambitions to encourage more people to get into sport as we won’t have the space! Hell bent on their development on the Green Belt, this would remove another barrier to allow them to bulldoze over pitches and open spaces. 

I urge all of you that care about our open spaces for sport to fill in the Government’s consultation here: www.gov.uk/government/consultations/reforms-to-the-statutory-consultee-system 
I’ll be writing to the Government too against this silly idea.

Best wishes,

Richard Holden

z3sBumGNvHLDHOLln0.text:
The Honoured Field Marshall, Born in Northern Ireland - Sir John Greer Dill. 

Along with my DUP colleague, Communities NI Minister Gordon Lyons MLA we visited Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia to lay a poppy wreath at the grave of Field Marshal Sir John Greer Dill, the Lurgan-born Ulster-Scot who is credited with establishing the 'Special Relationship' between the UK and USA during the Second World War.

On arrival, we were greeted by Arlington Cemetery and the Color Guard of the Saint Andrew's Society of Washington, DC, comprising UK and US military veterans.

Field Marshal Dill was Chief of the Imperial General Staff (professional head of the British Army) from 1940 to 1941. Subsequently posted to Washington DC as Churchill’s personal representative and Chief of the British Joint Staff Mission, he worked closely with US counterpart General George Marshall to establish what we now call the Special Relationship. 

After his death in November 1944, he was buried in Arlington by Joint Resolution of Congress and is the highest ranking non-American to be buried there. 
He was later honoured with a mounted statue, unveiled by President Harry S Truman, one of only two at the National Cemetery. 

At the unveiling of Dill's statue in Arlington, President Harry Truman said, 'I welcome this opportunity to remind my countrymen that the maintenance of a perfect understanding between the people of Great Britain and the United States is of great importance to the peace of the world - it is of the greatest importance to the peace of the world.

This statue will stand as a memorial not only to a man but to a remarkable Anglo-American relationship that bore fruit in a great victory--a really great victory'. 

Our wreath, bearing the crest of Northern Ireland, was supplied by the Oldpark/Cavehill Branch of the Royal British Legion. Thank you. 

Thank you too to the Ulster-Scots Agency for their support for this event and to the Color Guard of the Saint Andrew's Society of Wash

ad1EHcaTXfnqMNBKdC.text:
Halfway through our hols in Japan: 

After five days in Tokyo, stopping off for a few days each in Hakone, Takayama and then Kanazawa we have arrived in Kyoto. Without a word of a lie, this has to be one of the most interesting countries I have ever visited, and I’ve been to a few! Japan is truly a fascinating place in so many ways. Stunning forests and mountains, along with ultra modern metropoli,all seen as we barrel down the rail track @ 160+mph in a Shinkansen (bullet train).

Like many people I read James Clavell’s Shogun decades ago, and also watched the recent excellent drama on (I think Disney+), so it’s been really interesting to visit the shrines/temples (former Shinto, latter Buddhist) castles and gardens etc from that medieval era.

Aesthetically it’s such an attractive country; from the simple design of a railway station bench; to their tiny hotel bedrooms, cramped but precisely laid out; albeit our cpl of nights in Hakone were at a lovely traditional inn. Futons on the floor for sleeping but much more roomy. 

Equally there are also some deeply incongruous things such as a pirate ship which sails to and fro across Lake Ashi near Hakone - no, me neither 🤷‍♂️. Then, on visiting the 45th floor of the government building in Tokyo - astonishing view - when we got back to the bottom there was a sudden burst of scary music. On turning around, we saw that they’d shone an enormous image of Godzilla onto the side of the skyscraper - as you do 🤪

We’re both loving the whole experience - taking lots of buses and trains not forgetting the bullet train which is, frankly, awesome with loads of legroom, completely spotless and on time; so what’s not to like!

We’re now in Kyoto for the next five days, before visiting Hiroshima. Then it’s four days in Osaka, before gearing up for the 19 hr trip home. A long schlepp,to be sure, but this extraordinarily beautiful, impeccably polite, litter (and graffiti) free country makes it a journey well worth doing 🇯🇵😍

mSkc4EQZH3kADxXC1G.text:
I had the honour of attending the Service of Thanksgiving for the UDR, and all those who served and gave their lives to defend NI from the scourge of terrorism over the 23 years of the life of the regiment.

Since I became MP for East Antrim, it has been my honour to attend this service held in St Saviours Church in Connor each year.

The most poignant part of the service is when they read out the names of those who were murdered because they dared to serve in the UDR.

Last night I met the widow of one such soldier who was murdered at his own home, leaving his wife and three children. UDR soldiers were targets for terrorists 24 hours a day, not just when they were on patrol.

Over the lifetime of the regiment 40,000 men and women served in the UDR; 198 were murdered during their service but even after they had retired they were still targets. A further 62 were murdered even though they were no longer members.

Hundreds were left maimed as a result of injuries sustained because of terrorist murder attempts. 

It is important we remember the sacrifices made, and it was great to see so many veterans at the service proudly wearing their medals and remembering their fallen comrades.

As The Troubles fade from memory, it is sad to see that there is a generation growing up who don’t even know what the letters UDR stand for let alone the important work they did in securing peace in NI.

I thank Rev Ian Magowan and the local UDR ex members for their commitment to keeping alive this the memory of those who served our country so well in dark times.

We must never forget.

1vjmNcLGvwc1JeQhnT.text:
Before enjoying their Christmas dinner, Labour MPs should think long and hard about where that food actually comes from.

It didn't magically appear in Waitrose, or whatever vegan market they shop in - it was grown by British farmers, on British farms.

Those same farming families will soon be forced to sell their farm as a direct result of the changes being brought in by Labour. Who buys it up? Big multinationals, who care nothing for the land or our food security.

Farmers love their farms, and care for the land in a way nobody else could. I love my farm, it's my passion. If farmers go, the countryside we all love goes with them.

I still see people in the media, even MPs, failing to understand. Either they're doing so deliberately, or they're just thick.

The farm is only worth something once it's SOLD. Actual returns from farming are pitiful compared to the value of the land. If you're going to whack a bill on these grieving families based on what the farm is worth, they CAN'T pay it. They'll have to sell. How on earth do people not understand this? 

The impact of these changes may not be felt by the wider population next Christmas, or the one after that - but once significant numbers of farmers pass away, the British farming community will be changed forever. 

Farming is a very lonely business. Up early, out all day, often with just your own thoughts. All to scrape a living, in the hope that one day you can pass your farm down to your children - just as your parents did for you. That's the whole point. That's why farmers do what they do. 

Labour have snatched that dream away from thousands of farming families. I certainly won't forgive them, and the British farming community won't either.

Take a moment this Christmas to think about where your food comes from, the work that goes into providing it, and who is behind all of that.

British farmers, on British farms.

This Labour Government has taken a big step towards fixing decades of inequality in women’s healthcare. We’re making menopause part of routine NHS health checks and renewing the Women’s Health Strategy so women across the country finally get the care and respect they deserve.

Women represent more than half of the population, and between reproductive health, pregnancy and birth, and longer life expectancy, they are more likely to need medical care across their lifetime. But there’s a huge gender bias in medicine that means women’s symptoms often go under-recognised or misdiagnosed. Too many women have been ignored, dismissed or told to just get on with it. That ends now. 

If you’re between 40 and 74, your free NHS health check will soon include questions about menopause. That means nearly five million women will have access to better information, earlier support and proper treatment. It’s about time. Three-quarters of women experience symptoms that can last for years, yet many never get the help they need. By putting menopause front and centre, we’re and making sure women’s health is taken seriously.

Separately, as part of a wider package of investment to rebuild community pharmacies, the morning-after pill will soon be available for free from pharmacies across England. Right now, whether you can get it for free is a postcode lottery and requires visiting a GP or a sexual health clinic. Now women will be able to access this basic right at their local pharmacy. 

These changes are part of our wider mission to rebuild the NHS, bring more care into the community and make it work for everyone. We’ve already started cutting gynaecology waiting lists, introduced Jess’s Rule so GPs think again if they can’t find a diagnosis and committed to eliminating cervical cancer by 2040. It’s all part of a bigger plan to build an NHS fit for the future – one that listens, acts and delivers for everyone.

I met with Matt Scott‑Campbell from the Moors for the Future Partnership today to discuss the major new investment coming to our local peatlands, including the moors above Stalybridge, Mossley, and the areas overlooking Huddersfield Road.
 
Through their Moor Resilience 2030 programme, the Partnership has secured £25 million for peatland restoration across the Peak District and South Pennines to 2030, alongside green finance initiatives the Partnership is pioneering. This is a huge opportunity for our area.

Healthy peatland doesn’t just support wildlife, it also slows the flow of water off the hills, which can help reduce the risk of flooding and peatland fires for residents along Huddersfield Road and nearby communities. It improves water quality, stores carbon, and makes our moorland environment more resilient for the future.
 
Matt talked me through the restoration and monitoring work already under way, as well as habitat enhancement proposals under development with land managers for the moors above Stalybridge and Mossley - I’m keen to see this work on move forward so that people here can feel the full benefit.
 
Thank you to Matt for sharing the work going and I’m to the Moors for the Future Partnership for their long‑term commitment to protecting our moorland landscapes.

Allister comments after meeting on oil prices

Jim Allister MP said:

“Today’s meeting with Government ministers on the issue of fuel prices was, regrettably, largely disappointing.

"While there was no shortage of sympathetic words, there was very little in the way of concrete action for households and businesses struggling with the continuing cost of energy.

"Ministers gave no indication that they are prepared to remove the 5% VAT on home heating oil, despite the fact that so many households across Northern Ireland rely on it as their primary source of heat. Nor was there any commitment to retain the 5p per litre fuel duty rebate, a measure which has at least offered motorists some modest relief in recent years.

“Instead, much of the discussion focused on possible future regulatory changes, particularly in relation to the non-regulated wholesale fuel sector. While that may be worthy of examination, it offers no immediate help to families who are facing very real pressure today from the cost of filling their car or heating their home.

“Another unresolved issue concerns support mechanisms. In England there is a Crisis and Resilience Fund available to assist households facing acute financial pressure. Yet ministers were unable to clarify the extent to which any Barnett consequential will flow to Northern Ireland as a result.

“Ultimately, that means it will fall to the Northern Ireland Executive to decide whether to establish a parallel scheme to support local households.

“Given the scale of the pressures facing people, today’s meeting should have delivered far more than sympathetic words. What is required now is practical action that will genuinely ease the burden of high fuel and energy costs on the people of Northern Ireland.”

My Week in Westminster

I began Monday by speaking in Parliament to highlight the desperate need for greater SEND provision in Rossendale. The video of this is available on my Facebook page.

Later on, I attended a meeting of Red Wall Labour MPs, in which we discussed how to encourage Government and business investment into Northern towns. I'm glad to see we already have a lot of good things coming to our area, from the redevelopments in Bacup to improvements to the High Street in Rawtenstall, but I want to make sure our towns continue to stay a priority in the long-term. 

In the evening, we brought forward the Crime and Policing Bill, which will give the police new powers to tackle anti-social behaviour, shoplifting and street crime head on. From new Respect Orders to getting rid of the red tape stopping police officers from seizing stolen goods and bikes used for ASB, this law will empower our police to finally crack down on disorder. 

On Tuesday morning I met with the Tourism Alliance, to discuss how we can go about boosting the tourism industry in Rossendale and Darwen. Destination Darwen is a great example of how we can draw in regional and national tourism to the benefit of local businesses and communities. I'm keen to continue working with them on this. 

Later in the day, I met with representatives from Ceramics UK, a body that represents the entire ceramics industry in the UK, which has some members locally. We had a good conversation about what the Government can be doing to help the industry thrive and expand, and I'll be taking that forward in conversations with Ministers. 

I started Wednesday morning with the weekly Mission Champions meeting, discussing with Ministers how we can continue to deliver on our priorities. 

After Prime Minister's Questions, I spoke in the debate on the Government's Employment Rights bill, which is bringing forward new working rights for us all. Having run businesses for many years, I wanted to stress how these new rights

🅿️ ☕️ 🌳 🍰🅿️ Lake Meadows Parking - The Cafe in the Park 🅿️ 🫖 🌳 🥪🅿️ 

Cllr Phil Turner and I swung by Lakeview Palace Cafe for a coffee and a chat with Mike, the owners about how the new parking charges have affected his business.

Lake Meadows hosts so many facilities, the skate park and playgrounds, the fishing lake, Swimking Pool, bowls club and ‘Men’s Shed’. We all know how special Lake Meadows is and we absolutely should be encouraging people to visit their green spaces locally. 

Of course, the re-opened cafe has also been a part of that mix making it even more social – in fact, there’s many people that meet weekly in the café just to socialise.

That’s why it’s so disappointing, bizarre, verging on the vindictive that the Council is actively trying to put small businesses out of operation by killing off their footfall. This café only opened in February this year and now they are facing a massive challenge caused directly by the decision from Basildon Council. 

I could see the impact immediately when there were only half the normal staff plus Mark present. Sadly, the charges have put people off – something that customers were telling me. During our chat, everyone kept checking their watches and phones to ensure they didn’t overstay their parking! 

It’s very sad but not surprising to see these parking charges hammer a newly opened small business. We need to rally round our small business entrepreneurs and those they employ. Our council should be protecting our community spaces such as this fantastic café, so I’ll be making sure to step up my visits to help support Mike, and I hope the local community does too!

And as I said earlier, I’ll work alongside Phil, Cllr Andy Barnes, Cllr Andrew Schrader - Billericay East, Cllr Andy Baggott, Cllr Martyn Mordecai - Billericay East, Cllr Tony Hedley, Councillor Danny Lawrence - Billericay West, Cllr Kevin Blake and Cllr Richard Moore to get this perverse car park charging decision reversed. 

Best wishes,

Richard Hold

I want to put on the record my sincere thanks to Kemi Badenoch for following and supporting our Rape Gang Inquiry.

A number of Conservative MPs have attended, and I want to thank each and every one of them - particularly Esther McVey who has done so much work behind the scenes helping us put it all together.

Luke Myer, a Labour MP, also took the time to attend our inquiry. He did not have to do it, he knew he was probably going to get criticised. But he came, and he listened.

The Northern Irish patriots were of course supportive, and 
Carla Lockhart sat on the panel for one day. Again, it's appreciated.

Andrew Rosindell from Reform backed our motion on trafficking, as did one Lib Dem MP. James McMurdock  has also provided a huge amount of support.

The next steps are now this.

We still have a huge amount of evidence and testimonies that is to be released, and that will be done over the coming weeks.

Survivors came to tell their story, and we will help them do that in a safe and secure way.

The drafting of our report is already underway - that will take several weeks. I will update you all when I know more.

A target list for private prosecutions and civil litigation is being drawn up. This I am particularly determined about.

We will also be looking to push changes in the short term. I will have an update about this next week.

Our plan is to reopen our evidence submission portal so that more survivors can come forward - we will help them tell their story. If you have messaged us, keep in touch and it will be available soon.

Lots done, but there is so much more to do.

Our inquiry team are taking a rest this weekend. It is very well deserved.

Sarah Champion celebrates Labour Government’s funding boost for public health services in Rotherham

Sarah Champion has welcomed an increase in funding for public health services in Rotherham, the total amounting to an impressive £19,420,372 for the year 2025-26. This is part of the biggest real-terms increase, which amounts to £200 million nationally, after nearly a decade of reduced spending under the Conservatives.
 
Labour is committed to improving health outcomes across the country and building healthier communities. Through these public health grants, local health services will be able to deliver prevention and intervention programmes that are tailored to their residents.

Sarah Champion, Member of Parliament for Rotherham said:
 
“I welcome this uplift in spending to improve health outcomes across Rotherham. For too long, prevention has not been funded and I’m glad that is now changing, as prevention really is better than cure.  

“This funding will help reduce health inequalities, relieve pressure on the NHS and hopefully prevent people falling into ill health.
 
“This investment into our health services will make a real change locally and I look forward to seeing its implementation.
 
“The uplift from £18,434,695 to £19,420,372 for Rotherham, equates to £71.16 per constituent and a 4.95% increase from the year before, a much-needed investment into the people of our town.”

Child Practice Review into Neil Foden 

The findings of the Child Practice Review into the paedophile Neil Foden are deeply distressing and they must result in change. My thoughts are with the children whose lives were devastated by their abuse at the hands of their headteacher. 

Foden’s crimes were not only horrendous, they were calculated, and he cynically used his position of authority to engineer situations where he could exploit vulnerable children with impunity. What is most shocking is that there were multiple missed opportunities to intervene.

It is devastating to learn of the string of failures that led to the murder of Sara Sharif. 

Once again, the Family Court System was at the heart of a series of decisions that led to a child's death.

It is unthinkable that Sara should have been placed in her father's custody given the serious concerns about abuse and violence that had been raised against him but, having worked on the family courts system over many years, I know that decisions like these are not uncommon.

Women's Aid have previously found multiple examples of children and women who have been murdered at the hands of known abusers following the children being placed in unsafe contact arrangements.

The recent changes to allow greater transparency and reporting are an important step forward and will no doubt immediately begin to expose even more changes that need to be made. 

In the meantime, the Government should set out how we intend to reform the courts, at the very least by removing automatic parental rights for men who have committed murder or violent sexual abuse, as so many brave survivors have called for and for children to be considered victims of any domestic abuse in their household, regardless of whether it is physically perpetrated on them. In Sara's case, her mother and sibling were physical victims, but she was doubtless a victim too.

🚨PROTECTING HERITAGE IN 
BERKSWELL🚨

I have written to the Head of Planning at Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council, to register my formal objection to the outline planning application on the land off Windmill Lane in Berkswell.

The current iteration of the planning application demonstrates complete disregard for the impact of the development on Berkswell Windmill and its surrounding area.

Berkswell Windmill is an iconic Grade II star listed heritage site, which perfectly encapsulates the architecture and industry that makes our region so special. As we celebrate its 200th anniversary in 2026, it must be our priority to ensure that this cherished site is protected from intrusive development projects.

Most crucially, the approval of this planning application would set a dangerous precedent for the erosion of Green Belt and sites of historical significance in the future. This cannot be allowed to happen.

A special note of thanks to our local Conservative councillors who work so hard to protect our heritage and our greenbelt. 

Read my letter of objection below 👇

Over the last few months, I've been working with Help For Heroes  and the Royal British Legion  to support their campaigns for military compensation and pensions to be disregarded (not taken into account) when it comes to benefits – to ensure our veterans receive the full support they deserve.

I have submitted written questions and pushed Ministers on this, whilst it is great that military compensation is now disregarded for Universal Credit, each local council has the power to decide how it treats veterans and local benefits  - creating an unfair postcode lottery of support for our heroes.

South Tyneside Council have made the decision to disregard military compensation and pensions, which will ensure veterans living in South Tyneside get the full amount of benefits possible.

I hope that Gateshead Council will follow suit and ensure our veterans are treated with the respect and support they deserve.

I have written to Gateshead Council about this and I have submitted a follow up question to Ministers to ask them to instruct all Local Authorities to disregard the compensation and pensions of veterans and will keep pushing until all veterans get access to all the benefits they deserve.

The shutters came down on Connswater one last time at 6pm. A place that has been much more to our local community than simply bricks, mortar and a large glass front. 

It has served as a community hub, a meeting spot, the place where so many popped in to do their weekly shop, cash their wages, find their first Saturday job, grabbed a coffee, furnished the house or just for a quiet stroll from store to store. 

As I dandered through the centre in the final hour, the atmosphere was of quiet reflection, with many others taking their final walk and reminiscing of the shops that use to be in the various units on either side of the mall. 

A reminder of how much our communities change but on this occasion, a sad one. 

I joined Jonathan McAlpin from East Belfast Enterprise on the BBC’s Evening Extra with Mark Simpson this evening as we approached closing time - proudly wearing my most colourful odd socks for World Down Syndrome Day! A small but joyful act of celebration on a day otherwise tinged with sadness.

I welcome measures in today's Autumn Budget that bring help to our city. 

A higher minimum wage, ending the two‑child cap in Universal Credit, and freezes on rail fares and prescriptions ease pressure where wages are low and rents take nearly 40 percent of income. Money for school libraries and playgrounds matters in communities where child poverty is at 40 percent. Lower business rates for hospitality and leisure from next April support jobs and high streets.

On climate it is one step forward with charging investment, with hundreds of new chargepoints expected in Norwich, but two steps back with the scrapping of the ECO scheme, which makes fuel poverty and insulation problems harder to resolve.

Starting and running a business in 2025 Britain - let’s walk through it.

You’ve got a good idea, managed to save a few quid to invest and want to give it a go. Let’s say it’s a cafe. 

Generate wealth, create jobs and contribute to your local economy. Great idea. You just picked the wrong country to do it in.

Registering the damn thing is complicated enough, and that’s the easy bit. Next up is the bank account? You’re treated like a criminal and it takes week - opening a cafe, not a terrorist cell.

You manage to find a premise, good location. Oh, it costs a fortune. Rent through the roof and you’re forced to pay thousands to the council. For what? The filthy high street? The rapid customer service? Hmm. Yet another rip off. Inspections are a nightmare, it’s never-ending bureaucracy from people who have never created anything in their lives.

But somehow you get it off the ground and things go well. You need to expand, hire someone.

Ouch. PAYE, national insurance, pensions, HR policies, health and safety risk assessments. One wrong step and you’re facing an employment tribunal. Is it even worth the risk?

It’s becoming more and more expensive, and risky, to hire people? Why bother?

Maybe you try and get independent contracted help. Ah. IR35 puts a stop to that. We wouldn’t want any flexibility now, would we? That would make too much sense.

Your accountants already cost an absolute fortune. They’re bleeding you dry just so you comply with the layers and layers of regulations.

But let’s say it’s gone well, and your hard work is paying off. Turnover hits £90k. The dreaded VAT threshold. 

That means if you essentially then have to start charging VAT. That means everything gets 20% more expensive for your customers. Or you are forced to absorb the costs. Or you deliberately make less money to stay below the threshold. Just brilliant.

Maybe you want to keep the cafe open later? Serve some alcohol? Have some music on?

More licences. More costs. More inspections. M

𝑾𝒆 𝒘𝒊𝒍𝒍 𝒓𝒆𝒎𝒆𝒎𝒃𝒆𝒓 - This morning, I had the real privilege of attending a service in Lurgan, where a new memorial was unveiled to honour Field Marshal Sir John Greer Dill, a true legend born in Lurgan on Christmas Day 1881. 

Dill’s roots in Lurgan ran deep—his father managed the local Ulster Bank, and his family had longstanding ties to the region’s linen and Presbyterian traditions. Over the course of his distinguished career, Dill would go on to play a pivotal role in World War II.

As Chief of the Imperial General Staff, he led British forces through some of the war’s darkest days. Later, he was sent to Washington, D.C., where his diplomatic skill and integrity established the "Special Relationship" between the UK and USA. His close partnership with US General George Marshall built a vital bridge between the Allies, uniting them in purpose.

Today was a fitting day to remember Dill, as it marked the 80th anniversary of his passing. It was a pleasure to meet members of the Dill family, who had travelled to be part of this commemoration. Field Marshal Dill’s legacy continues to inspire, and he is one of only two soldiers at Arlington National Cemetery to be honoured with an equestrian statue—a rare tribute to a Lurgan-born legend.

A heartfelt thanks to the RBL Lurgan and Brownlow Branch and ABC Council for their efforts in making this lasting tribute possible.

Lest we forget!

We have some of the best lawyers, barristers and judges in the world. But we’ve got a problem. I have concerns that some judges have strongly held beliefs which have the potential to subvert the impartiality of the judiciary.

More than 30 sitting immigration judges have former links to the very activist groups that have ground our court system to a halt. Can judges who have supported and volunteered for organisations and charities such as Bail for Immigration Detainees – whose stated policy is to “work towards a world free of immigration detention” and where no one is “deported from their homes” – be considered to be neutral and unbiased?

Maybe they can, but it is time that we raise these questions. These are not isolated examples; they point to a judiciary where activism and adjudication seem to go together.

The problem goes beyond the effect of any decisions these judges have reached. The rule of law relies on the public having confidence in the impartiality of the judiciary – that the person hearing the cases they bring appears to be a neutral arbitrator.

If judges are tweeting political opinions that directly touch on the policies they’re charged with mediating upon, that confidence is shattered. That’s why I feel so strongly that these people should have no place in our justice system.

Plan to overhaul appointment of judges

So, yesterday, I announced a bold new approach for how judges are appointed and how they’re removed. At present, judges are appointed and disciplined by quangos.

The first problem is that the Judicial Conduct Investigation Office routinely hands biased judges warnings rather than dismissing them.

The second problem goes much deeper, though – who picks the judges in our courts. Tony Blair handed the job to the Judicial Appointments Commission. Many of the Commissioners are doing a good job, others less so.

Our new plan would see judges appointed again by the Lord Chancellor – an elected minister accountable to the public. A new vetti

It’s time to restore respect.

When we left the EU on 31 Dec 2020, the UK became an independent coastal state. Since then, the Scottish Fishing Fleet have been able get better annual deals with other coastal states like Norway 🇳🇴 , Iceland 🇮🇸 and Faroe 🇫🇴 than we ever would have got if we had remained as an EU member state.

However the deal meant continued automatic and free access to our waters by EU vessels. This concession was negotiated to allow the EU fishing industry an ‘adjustment period’ before the UK took FULL control, only allowing boats to fish in our waters on the basis of annual negotiations.

The EU will want another ‘multi-year’ agreement through which they catch more fish in UK waters than they do in their own. The Labour Government negotiators must stand firm against this and ensure that any future access to UK waters is agreed only in annual negotiations, the same as any other coastal state.

Elspeth Macdonald:

“Wild capture fisheries in our EEZ are naturally renewable – they don’t need chemicals and fertilisers to secure our food security – just skilled, knowledgeable and experienced fishermen who have dedicated their working lives to harvesting these resources efficiently and sustainably.
 
“Giving up rights to decide who fishes in our EEZ, and when and how, would be a betrayal of UK sovereignty. We don’t give the EU access to the UK EEZ to build windfarms or extract oil and gas, so why would we give away our hugely valuable fisheries resources?

“In addition, the UK must not allow itself to be threatened by the EU on market access. No other fisheries agreement in the north-east Atlantic couples access to fisheries with access to markets, and the UK Government must resist this strongly.”

Scottish Fishermen's Federation

Today we honour the service and sacrifice of all those that have defended our freedoms and protected our way of life. 

This morning, I am joining the Annual Remembrance Parade hosted by Blackpool Sixth Form’s Protective Service students and on Sunday, I stood at the cenotaph and laid a wreath to pay my respects and those of every Blackpool South resident. In Parliament’s Remembrance Garden, a tribute has been planted to honour all those gave their lives for us and those who continue to do so from Blackpool. These moments are deeply personal to me.

My grandad Dougie Webb served in the Second World War, bravely fighting fascism across Europe. Today and often, I think of the millions of brave souls like him who selflessly answered the call of duty to serve and protect our country. 

The stories of those who served should never fade. We remember them. We honour them. And in the work we do now to support those who served, we prove that remembrance is far more than a moment of silence once a year.

Drive down almost any country road and you see the same thing. 

Litter lining the roads. Plastic caught in hedges. Fast food packaging scattered across the grass. Crisp packets fluttering in the wind. Rusting energy drink cans just laying about. What message are we sending to children as they watch the rubbish pile up? It’s disgusting.

Nobody talks about it. We’ve just accepted it as normal. It infuriates me.

There was a time in this country when this level of disrespect would have been unthinkable. People took pride in where they lived. There was a clear expectation that public spaces would be kept clean and orderly, and that those who did otherwise would face consequences.

This was not that long ago. The decline has rapidly accelerated. Britain is increasingly resembling a third world country, and I do not like it. Immigration from said cultures has evidently played a large part. I’ll get abused for saying it, but it’s true. We all know it.

Once we start accepting visible decline in the small things, it rarely stops there. It hasn’t stopped there. It will get worse and worse and worse. The filth will pile up.

Britain should not look like this. It is not unreasonable to expect clean streets, clear roadsides, and public spaces that people can take pride in. Is that too much to ask for? I think not.

A Restore Britain Government would not tolerate it. Proper enforcement of littering and fly-tipping laws. Visible consequences for those who degrade our countryside. Deportation for foreign fly-tippers. Investment in keeping streets, roads, and public areas clean. Compulsory litter picking for non-violent offenders and healthy benefit claimants who consistently refuse work.

Most importantly?

A cultural shift.

Britain does not have to be a dumping ground.

We will set an example to our children and grandchildren.

There is now a political party that will clean up our country.

Real people. Family businesses. The sort of places that keep towns and villages alive.

They are running out of road, and the business rates change will be the end of the road for many.

They’ve absorbed blow after blow over the last few decades and kept going anyway. But this will be the end for many. A sad, bitter end.

Rising rents. Rising supplier costs. Rising insurance. Endless compliance. Paperwork that grows every year but adds absolutely zero value.

They dealt with all the lockdown bullshit.

Forced closures. Confusing rules. Constant U-turns. Damaging loans. ‘Following’ the science, remember?

Many got no proper support due to the structure of their businesses. They battled on.

People remortgaged homes, drained savings, worked unpaid - just to keep the doors intact so they could reopen when finally allowed.

When restrictions were lifted, it wasn’t normal. Customers poorer, costs stayed high, footfall patchy.

Then the energy costs blowing up after the Ukraine war. Still bleeding the business dry.

And now, on top of all of that, they’re staring down a business rates revaluation that could be the final straw. Not because their business is suddenly thriving or profits are surging, but because a formula has made some impossibly complicated recalculations.

For hospitality, there is no escape. A pub can’t go remote. A cafe can’t move to a warehouse.

They have to be there. In the town, paying extortionate business rates.

This, of course, is all after higher operating costs from the first Reeves budget. NI changes were punishing for these businesses. Absolutely punishing.

jCCGJqWnAh9l7tXyJg.text:
Meet Call-sign 'Dev'

Dev – short for Developer - goes backwards and forwards between the battlefields of eastern Ukraine and his unit’s tech hub in what looks like a detached, run-down house in the suburbs of a frontline town. Dev is working on the latest iterations of drones. He is the chief technical officer for a unit, Achilles, that specialises in them.

I write about him and Achilles in my book, The New Total War, to show how Ukraine is pioneering drone innovation to defend itself againast the Russian invasion.

At the end of last year when I met Dev, the ‘drone zone’ - the area in which you were in danger from battlefield drones - was 10km from no man's land. Now that drone kill zone can stretch up to 30kms from the frontline. It's also begining to be saturated by drones, at their most basic quadcopters carrying bombs weighing between 2 and 10 kilos, looking for targets: cars, soldiers military equipment, and even civilians. 

This weekend a civilian train was struck by a drone in northern Ukraine.

When I met him, Dev was studying fibre optics, drones linked by a super thin, 2mm, cable, which are resistant to Electronic Warfare (EW) counter-measures. Six months later, these are now so prevalent that birds are making nests out of the miles upon miles of fibre optic cable that litter front line areas.

“The drones can hit the target and EW can’t cope with it." Dev says of fibre optics. The problem, however, is price. “10km of fibre optic cable is more expensive than the drone,” he says. More cost equals fewer drones. And more weight equals less range. The trade-offs are continuous.

The New Total War, out now.

Picture: Annabel Moeller

JfuFHpeWaXYZ2s4zNR.text:
In a week that sees a grim milestone in Ukraine I chatted to Ukrainian Action in Parliament yesterday. 

A charity set up here and in the US, they have coordinated an incredible 69
Convoys of aid into Ukraine since the war began. 

One of their most active local groups is the Devon group operating from Stoke Gabriel, who I met last year at the Dartmouth Food Festival. 

It was great to hear from Natasha Hartman and Phil Gardner how valued the Devon aid convoys are. 

On arrival in Ukraine they leave the trucks in Ukraine along with the aid, and travel home in trains and planes - so the Ukrainians can use the vehicles. 348 so far have been donated. 

Natasha told me someone recently drove all the way in a cherry picker, which is now being used in Zaporizhzhia. 

The charity also runs retreats for veterans and their families in the Carpathian Mountains, and thanks to donations of equipment they have taught disabled veterans to ski. The rehabilitation work with veterans and their families is likely to continue long into the future even if a peace deal is secured. 

Really inspiring work, and I look forward to catching up with the Stoke Gabriel crew again soon - and maybe even joining a convoy.

I had the pleasure of taking part in the Energy Research Accelerator roundtable, Next Generation Nuclear: Powering Britain’s Energy Future, in Portcullis House, Westminster.

It was a focused, question led discussion on how large reactors, SMRs, AMRs and fusion can strengthen the UK’s energy security, affordability and net zero pathway, alongside a renewables led grid. We also dug into the practical enablers that will decide whether we succeed: regulation that is fit for purpose, the skills pipeline, supply chain readiness, and public confidence.

These themes resonate strongly with my work at NEMO - Nuclear Energy Maritime Organization where we are focused on ensuring the right international frameworks are in place for nuclear applications at sea, and on bringing regulators and industry together early to reduce friction and accelerate safe deployment.

I am also proud to support this agenda through my role as a Board Director and Trustee of the Nuclear Institute - UK, championing the skills, professionalism and standards the UK needs to deliver at pace.

Thank you to Chris Moore for excellent chairing, and to Shawn Coles FCIM and the Green Infrastructure Week team for convening such a timely and constructive session.

It was also a pleasure to take part alongside Nick King, Trudy Harrison, Andrew Bowie, Mark Rouse, Zion Lights, Oliver Parsons, David Cole FREng, Abigail, Gary Jones, Claire Young, Tim Gregory, Amanda Baxendale, David Brinson, Tom Davis and many more.

Supporters of Nuclear Energy - SONE

#Nuclear #EnergySecurity #NetZero
